rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation and changing lengths of night and day are cosmic proofs of a wise, powerful, knowing maker and guide to Islam and divine oneness.
rows.anchor: المعنى جعلنا الملوين بهيآتهما وتعاقبهما واختلافهما في الطول والقصر على وتيرة عجيبة آيتين تدلان على أن لهما صانعا حكيما قادرا عليما

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam links this verse to the prior one as worldly blessing following the Qur’an’s religious blessing; time, like scripture, needs both of its complementary parts for full benefit.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى لما بين في الآية المتقدمة ما أوصل إلى الخلق من نعم الدين وهو القرآن أتبعه بيان ما أوصل إليهم من نعم الدنيا

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Because humans move hastily from state to state, the Imam says the world likewise moves between light and darkness and the moon’s waxing and waning.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى وصف الإنسان بكونه عجولا أي منتقلا من صفة إلى صفة ومن حالة إلى حالة بين أن كل أحوال العالم كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third coherence explanation reprises the opening account: reporting these created signs is Qur’anic guidance that directs people to infer from them.
rows.anchor: الثالث نحو ما نقلناه أولا ولعله الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night comes first because day emerges from it, Arabic lunar months begin with its appearances, and the day’s purpose follows it directly; the surah also opened with a night journey.
rows.anchor: وتقديم الليل لمراعاة الترتيب الوجودي إذ منه ينسلخ النهار وفيه تظهر غرر الشهور العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jaʿala can mean transforming, taking two objects, or creating, taking one; “two signs” is a prospective circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: والجعل على ما نقل عن السمين بمعنى التصيير متعد لاثنين أو بمعنى الخلق متعد لواحد و ( آيتين ) حال مقدرة

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani objects that “made” as transformation implies night and day first existed in another state; the answer treats this as a familiar figurative idiom, a reading Abu Hayyan favors.
rows.anchor: واستشكل الأول الكرماني بأنه يستدعي أن يكون الليل والنهار موجودين على حالة ثم انتقلا منها إلى أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appositional reading of “the sign of night” identifies the night itself with its erased, darkened sign, where nothing is visible.
rows.anchor: الإضافة هنا وفيما بعد إما بيانية كما في إضافة العدد إلى المعدود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ is explanatory: erasing night’s sign and brightening day are components of making night and day into signs, not later events.
rows.anchor: والفاء تفسيرية لأن المحو المذكور وما عطف عليه ليسا مما يحصل عقيب جعل الجديدين آيتين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes erasure literally: God removed the night sign’s established light, leaving darkness; the author ultimately endorses this interpretation.
rows.anchor: المعول عليه ما في الكشاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative makes night’s erasure the removal of darkness by light, preserving the literal sense of erasure, but the author finds its explanation of the contrast and benefit overcomplicated and ill-suited.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى ما فيه من التكلف وأن المقام لا يلائمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Day’s sign made seeing” means illuminating; it can be causal figurative attribution, a relational adjective, or “made its people see,” with God as the true agent.
rows.anchor: أي مضيئة فهو مجاز بعلاقة السببية أو الإسناد مجازي

rows.speaker: قتادة وعلي بن الحسين
rows.claim: Qatada and ʿAli b. al-Husayn read “مبصرة” with open mīm and ṣād, a verbal noun used adjectivally, like place adjectives.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة وعلي بن الحسين رضي الله تعالى عنهما ( مبصرة ) بفتح الميم والصاد

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda’s explanation takes the word in its lexical, transitive sense: the day’s sign makes people seeing, rather than relying on figurative attribution.
rows.anchor: وروي ذلك عن أبي عبيدة وهو معنى وضعي لا مجازي

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: If the night and day signs are the moon and sun, one can supply “lights” as the signs’ referent, or construe night and day adverbially as containing the two signs; Abu Hayyan favors the reversed object analysis.
rows.anchor: كما استظهره أبو حيان وجعل الليل والنهار نصبا على الظرفية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the moon once shone like the sun, then its light was erased; its dark markings remain as traces of that erasure.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في الآية أنه قال

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reports that sun and moon each began with seventy parts of light; sixty-nine lunar parts were transferred to the sun, leaving one for the moon.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبد بن حميد وغيره عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad b. Kaʿb al-Qurazi says there had been a sun at night and one by day; God erased the night sun, leaving the moon’s dark mark.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن محمد بن كعب القرظي

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
rows.claim: In a report from Saʿid al-Maqburi, ʿAbd Allah b. Salam asks the Prophet about lunar darkness; the Prophet says there were two suns and identifies the mark as the erasure.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد المقبري أن عبد الله بن سلام سأل النبي

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report with a weak chain from Ibn ʿAbbas says Gabriel swept the moon’s face three times when it was a sun, extinguishing its light but leaving radiance.
rows.anchor: بسند واه عن ابن عباس مرفوعا أن الله تعالى خلق شمسين من نور عرشه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says the moon is created dim and has no inherent light, so the fāʾ explains its nature; another says its reflected light visibly wanes to disappearance, making the fāʾ sequential.
rows.anchor: قيل محو القمر إما خلقه كمدا مطموس النور غير مشرق بالذات

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam gives two readings of lunar erasure: gradual waning to disappearance or lunar surface spots; he prefers waning because it explains the practical purposes of seeking livelihood and counting years.
rows.anchor: وذكر الإمام في محوه قولين أحدهما نقص نوره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says a sound Prophetic report for the earlier account of lunar erasure would preclude calling the alternative preferable; the moon’s changing appearance is obvious to observers.
rows.anchor: متى دل أثر صحيح عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على ما ذكرناه أولا لا ينبغي أن يدعى أن غيره أولى

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam rejects reflected images of mountains and seas as the cause of lunar spots: mirror images would shift with viewing position, and a reflecting moon is not suited to visual illusion.
rows.anchor: أما أولا فلأن الأشباح لا تتحفظ هيآتها مع حركة المرآة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: An elemental screen is also rejected: it would vary with viewpoint, while air and fire are transparent and vapor or smoke would not persist.
rows.anchor: وأما إن كان ذلك بسبب سائر فذلك السائر إما أن يكون عنصريا أو سماويا

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam accepts a celestial explanation: tiny nearby heavenly bodies, dark or dimmer than the moon, could collectively make its visible spots.
rows.anchor: وأما إن كان الساتر سماويا فهو الحق وذلك إنما يكون لقيام أجسام سماوية قريبة المكان جدا من القمر

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam argues that moon phases affect worldly conditions such as tides and medical crises, and their recurrence yields lunar months and years, supporting the phase interpretation’s stated benefits.
rows.anchor: مثل أحوال البحار في المد والجزر ومثل أحوال البحرانات على ما يذكره الأطباء

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: If lunar markings are made of the moon’s own substance, the Imam says their difference from bright areas still needs an external cause; celestial bodies are not altered by elemental matter.
rows.anchor: وإما أن تكون تلك المواضع مساوية الماهية لجرم القمر فحينئذ يمتنع اختصاصها بتلك الآثار إلا بسبب خارجي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the theory that fire wore away the moon’s surface: that would eventually destroy it, successive observations contradict this, and the moon is far from fire.
rows.anchor: وبذلك أبطل قول من قال : إن ذلك المحو

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam argues that if fire touched the moon’s carrier, fire’s motion would carry it eastward, but shooting stars usually move west; fire’s own motion is straight, not circular.
rows.anchor: بدليل أن النار لو كانت ملاقية لحامله لتحركت بحركته إلى المشرق

rows.speaker: الفلاسفة
rows.claim: The philosophers’ latest proposal is that dim celestial bodies are embedded in the moon like spots; selective placement among homogeneous parts points to a choosing creator.
rows.anchor: آخر ما ذكره الفلاسفة في ذلك أنه ارتكن في وجه القمر أجسام قليلة الضوء

rows.speaker: بعض أهل الآثار
rows.claim: Some traditionists claim the lunar marks spell “There is no god but God,” “Jamil,” or another inscription; the author says none of these claims is reliable.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعض أهل الآثار أنه مكتوب في وجه القمر لا إله إلا الله وقيل لفظ جميل

rows.speaker: أهل الهيئة الجديدة
rows.claim: Modern astronomers claim the moon has earthly mountains, valleys, trees, and seas; they identify smooth marks with seas and mottled areas with rough land, and infer possible inhabitants on the moon and other planets.
rows.anchor: أن القمر كالأرض فيه الجبال والوهاد والأشجار والبحار وأنهم شاهدوا ذلك في أرصادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author dismisses lunar-world speculation as unsupported and contrary to philosophical principles, based on unverified visual impressions; he allows that God could create forms resembling what they imagine.
rows.anchor: كلامهم في هذا الباب مخالف لأصول الفلسفة ولا برهان لهم عليه سوى السفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that vast planets must be inhabited would also imply inhabitants in larger interstellar spaces; the author answers that angels may populate the heavens and moon, and advises ignoring such speculation.
rows.anchor: على أنا نقول قد جاء أطت السماء وحق لها أن تئط ما فيها موضع قدم إلا وفيه ملك راكع أو ساجد

rows.speaker: الآمدي
rows.claim: Al-Amidi is cited against treating the sun as inherently luminous and the moon’s light as borrowed from it: both are philosophical claims without a scriptural basis.
rows.anchor: وقد عد الجل من العلماء ذلك في الحدسيات

rows.speaker: الآمدي
rows.claim: Al-Amidi says God could create light in a dark-bodied sun at the observed times, or its light could come from higher stars hidden by dark celestial bodies.
rows.anchor: وما المانع من كونها سوداء الجرم والله تعالى يخلق فيها النور في أوقات مشاهدتنا لها

rows.speaker: الآمدي
rows.claim: Even if the sun shines inherently, Al-Amidi says the moon need not borrow its light: God may create variable lunar light, or one face may shine while the moon rotates synchronously in its orbit.
rows.anchor: فلا نسلم أن نور القمر مستفاد منها وأما المانع من كون الرب تعالى يخلق فيه النور في وقت دون وقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says combining eclipses with lunar phases and apparent distances confirms borrowed sunlight; the reply is that an upper body, not necessarily Earth, could eclipse the moon, and no proof excludes this.
rows.anchor: وأورد أنه إذا ضم الخسوف إلى الزيادة والنقصان قربا وبعدا لا يتم ما ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “So you may seek” attaches to the daylight sign: daylight enables people to seek provision, which is called divine bounty because livelihood cannot be acquired at night.
rows.anchor: لتبتغوا ( متعلق بقوله تعالى ( وجعلنا آية النهار )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Provision is a gift of divine nurture, not something owed for human effort; effort is only an ordinary cause and not a necessary condition for provision.
rows.anchor: على أن ليس للعبد في تحصيل الرزق تأثير سوى الطلب وإنما الاعطاء إلى الله سبحانه لا بطريق الوجوب عليه تعالى

rows.speaker: القائل
rows.claim: An unattributed poem supports the point that provision arrives whether one pursues it or sits still.
rows.anchor: لقد علمت وما الاشراف من خلقي أن الذي هو رزقي سوف يأتيني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “So you may know” depends on both erasing night’s sign and illuminating day; knowledge comes from their differences, lights, succession, motions, positions, and other states.
rows.anchor: كلا الفعلين أعني محو آية الليل وجعل آية النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Counting years serves religious and worldly needs; calculation concerns the months, nights, days, and other times within them that organize practical interests.
rows.anchor: التي يتعلق بها غرض علمي لإقامة مصالحكم الدينية والدنيوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes calculation as ordinary transactions and emphasizes learning by night or moon in light of 2:189; the author replies that solar and lunar years are both used.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أن الظاهر المناسب أن المراد لتعلموا بالليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Number precedes calculation because it gives a general count before detailed accounting, is more basic than compound calculation, and can be the highest level of gratitude in context.
rows.anchor: وتقديم العدد على الحساب من أن الترتيب بين متعلقيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Everything” means whatever people need for worldly life and the afterlife beyond the night-day signs and their benefits; it is accusative by an implied verb explained by “We detailed.”
rows.anchor: يفتقرون إليه في معاشكم ومعادكم سوى ما ذكر من جعل الليل والنهار آيتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Detail means complete clarification, emphasized by its verbal noun: the Qur’an explains everything without ambiguity and is guidance to the straightest path.
rows.anchor: والتفصيل من الفصل بمعنى القطع والمراد به الإبانة التامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Every human” is syntactically like “everything” above and refers to each morally accountable person.
rows.anchor: أي وألزمنا كل إنسان مكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person’s ṭāʾir is the voluntary deed apportioned to him, good or evil, as though it flew to him from the hidden nest of destiny.
rows.anchor: أي عمله الصادر منه باختياره حسبما قدر له خير أكان أو شرا كأنه طار إليه من عش الغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bird metaphor comes from Arabs’ divination: a bird released on a journey was lucky if it passed left to right (sāniḥ) and unlucky right to left (bāriḥ), so deeds and decree became figurative “birds.”
rows.anchor: كانوا يتفاءلون بالطير ويسمونه زجرا فإذا سافروا ومر بهم طير زجروه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas interprets ṭāʾir here as a person’s deed; Mujahid is also reported to hold this interpretation.
rows.anchor: وتفسيره بالعمل هنا مروي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid likewise interprets ṭāʾir as the person’s deed, according to a report in al-Bayhaqi’s Shuʿab al-Iman.
rows.anchor: ورواه البيهقي في شعب الإيمان عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes ṭāʾir one’s primordial allotted share, assigned according to what one merits in God’s eternal knowledge.
rows.anchor: وفسره بعضهم بما وقع للعبد في القسمة الأزلية الواقعة حسب استحقاقه في العلم الأزلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In his neck” pictures an inescapable, permanent attachment, like a collar or shackle; the neck is visible and can stand for the whole person.
rows.anchor: تصوير لشدة اللزوم وكمال الارتباط

rows.speaker: حذيفة بن أسيد
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says an angel forms the fetus after four months, records its features, happiness or misery, lifespan, provision, trials, and deeds, then hangs its book at its neck until God’s decree.
rows.anchor: عن حذيفة بن أسيد سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fetal-record report appears to make “neck” literal and ṭāʾir the written book; Anas is explicitly reported to interpret it that way, and the author accepts sound reports while deferring their manner.
rows.anchor: وأن الطائر عبارة عن كتاب الذي كتب فيه ما كتب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says every newborn has a leaf at its neck recording whether the child is blessed or wretched, supporting an unrestricted reading of “every human”; the verse’s ending seems to limit it to the accountable.
rows.anchor: أخرجه أبو داؤد في كتاب القدر وابن جرير وابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: مجاهد والحسن وأبو رجاء
rows.claim: Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Abu Rajaʾ read ṭāʾir as ṭayr; another reading gives sukūn to the nūn in ʿunuq.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد والحسن وأبو رجاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emerging book is the person’s record of deeds for the reckoning; its accusative can be the object of “bring forth” or a circumstantial description of the omitted object, the bird.
rows.anchor: والبعث للحساب ﴿ كتابا ﴾ ( هي صحيفة عمله

rows.speaker: يعقوب ومجاهد وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Yaʿqub, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin read the verb actively with “book” accusative as a circumstantial phrase, taking the bird as its subject.
rows.anchor: ويعضد ذلك قراءة يعقوب ومجاهد وابن محيصن

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar’s passive reading with accusative “book” also supports a circumstantial construction; other variants make “book” the passive subject or active subject.
rows.anchor: وكذا قراءة أبي جعفر ( ويخرج )

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy b. Kaʿb’s reading says each person’s bird “reads it on Judgment Day as a book,” explicitly identifying the bird with the record.
rows.anchor: عن هرون قال في قراءة أبي بن كعب

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو جعفر والجحدري والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Jahdari, and in one report al-Hasan read “it is delivered to him,” with a passive intensive form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وأبو جعفر والجحدري والحسن بخلاف عنه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan likens the record to a person’s open ledger kept by two noble angels, one on each side; it is folded at death, placed on the neck in the grave, then brought out at resurrection.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير عن الحسن أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Read your book” is what the person is told; the clause may be an adjective, circumstantial clause, or independent statement.
rows.anchor: بتقدير يقال له ذلك وهذه الجملة إما صفة أو حال أو مستأنفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “yourself suffices,” the mainstream parses “yourself” as the subject with an added bāʾ; the address yāʾ is a separation marker, sometimes omitted in poetry.
rows.anchor: وكفى فعل ماض وبنفسك فاعله والياء سيف خطيب وجاء إسقاطها

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: Two poetic examples use “كَفى” to show the construction, including a line where gray hair and Islam suffice as an admonition.
rows.anchor: كفى الشيب والإسلام للمرء ناهيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians note the verb lacks feminine agreement with “nafs”; although agreement can vary for a nonhuman feminine subject after an added preposition, analogous verbs do show it.
rows.anchor: ولم تلحق الفعل علامة التأنيث وإن كان مثله تلحقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some instead make the subject “sufficiency” or treat kafā as an imperative-like particle with an implicit addressee, so the bāʾ is not extra; the majority prefers the earlier parse.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قيل إن فاعل كفى ضمير يعود على الاكتفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Today” is a time adverb; ḥasīban is either specification or circumstantial, and “against you” fits the sense of an accountant who counts a person’s acts.
rows.anchor: ( اليوم ) ظرف لكفى و ( حسيبا ) تمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥasīb may mean accountant or sufficient witness; describing the feminine nafs with masculine ḥasīb is explained by the male-associated role, by treating nafs as person, or by the adjective’s pattern.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد بالنفس الذات فكأنه قيل كفى بك حسيبا عليك

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil takes “yourself” to mean the bodily limbs that testify against a person when he denies his deeds; the author calls this contrary to the apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل أن المراد بالنفس الجوارح فإنها تشهد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: When reciting the verse, al-Hasan says God has dealt fairly with a person by making him the judge of himself.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أنه كان إذا قرأ الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command applies to believers and unbelievers; al-Suddi’s account of an unbeliever asking to judge himself does not restrict the verse to unbelievers.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يقال ذلك للمؤمن والكافر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reports that on Judgment Day even one who could not read in worldly life will read the record.
rows.anchor: ويقرأ في ذلك اليوم كما روي عن قتادة من لم يكن قارئا في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes the believer first seeing sins in the record, fearing ruin, then finding them forgiven and reading good deeds with growing joy and light.
rows.anchor: وجاء أن المؤمن يقرأ أولا سيآته وحسناته في ظهر كتابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corresponding account says an unbeliever sees good deeds rejected, is darkened with grief, and then reads his sins; the report cites the rejected deeds and his lament over the book.
rows.anchor: وأما الكافر فيقرأ أولا حسناته وسيآته في ظهر كتابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mystical-philosophical interpretation identifies the book with the soul bearing hidden imprints of deeds, revealed after bodily separation; the author says this is remote from the plain sense and treats resurrection as a lesser resurrection.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم الكتاب بالنفس المتنفسة بآثار الأعمال ونشره وقراءته بظهور ذلك له ولغيره

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam says the narrated outward events are true and the verse can also bear spiritual meanings, so one should affirm both; Khafaji says this need not contradict transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: إن الحق أن الأحوال الظاهرة التي وردت فيها الروايات حق وصدق لا مرية فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author doubts that the spiritual reading is an apparent meaning or that Qatada’s statement supports it; reading the illiterate person’s record literally is itself an alternative interpretation.
rows.anchor: ولعل قتادة وأمثاله من سلف الأمة لا يخطر لهم أمثال هذه التأويلات ببال

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam’s first coherence link is that the Qur’an has supplied needed proofs of divine oneness, prophethood, and resurrection, leaving no excuse when people face judgment.
rows.anchor: كل ما يحتاج إليه من دلائل التوحيد والنبوة والمعاد قد صار مذكورا

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Second, God’s many religious and worldly benefits require service and obedience, so each person is questioned about words and deeds.
rows.anchor: أوصل إلى الخلق أصناف الأشياء النافعة لهم في الدين والدنيا

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Third, since God created humans to worship and made material things useful for them, judgment asks whether each person obeyed or rebelled.
rows.anchor: وما خلقت الجن والإنس إلا ليعبدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author offers another link: the preceding passage describes God’s book of guidance, while this one describes the human record that omits no small or great deed; a person’s record reflects whether he followed that first book.
rows.anchor: إن فيما تقدم شرح حال كتاب الله تعالى المتضمن بيان النافع والضار من الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse summarizes that the Qur’an guides to the straightest way: whoever follows its commands and avoids its prohibitions benefits himself, while the one who strays bears the loss.
rows.anchor: من اهتدى بهدايته وعمل بما في تضاعيفه من الأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No bearer bears another’s burden” reinforces that deeds remain attached to their doer and blocks the excuse that ancestors or leaders will assume responsibility.
rows.anchor: تأكيد للجملة الثانية أي لا تحمل نفس حاملة للوزر وزر نفس أخرى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the verse came down about al-Walid b. al-Mughira, who told people to reject Muhammad and promised to bear their sins.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنها نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: There is no contradiction with verses assigning a share to good or bad intercession and extra burdens to misleaders: people receive the consequence of their own intercession or misguidance, not another’s original deed.
rows.anchor: لأنه في الحقيقة انتفاع بحسنة نفسه وتضرر بسيئته

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha challenged Ibn ʿUmar’s report that the dead are punished for relatives’ wailing as apparently charging one person with another’s offense; the author answers that the dead person may have ordered it.
rows.anchor: ولهذه الآية طعنت عائشة رضي الله عنها في صحة خبر ابن عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other answers take the “dead” as a dying person distressed by family wailing, or explain that Aisha rejected charging a clan with blood money because such liability is an independent legal duty, not punishment for its own act.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بالميت المحتضر مجازا

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi argues that children of polytheists cannot be punished for their parents’ sins; some say the verse was revealed about them, which the author denies.
rows.anchor: واستدل بها الجبائي على أن أطفال المشركين لا يعذبون

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A weak report from Aisha says Khadija asked about polytheist children: an initial answer associates them with their fathers, then after Islam’s establishment the Prophet cites this verse and says they are upon the innate nature or in Paradise.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن عبد البر في التمهيد بسند ضعيف عن عائشة

rows.speaker: الصعب بن جثامة
rows.claim: In a sound report from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ṣaʿb b. Jaththama asks about killing enemy children in a night raid; the Prophet says they are of them, interpreted by opponents as worldly legal status such as enslavement.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الشيخان وأصحاب السنن وغيرهم عن ابن عباس قال : حدثني الصعب بن جثامة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Some scholars suspend judgment about polytheist children; Abu Hanifa is among them. Another view says some enter Paradise and some Hell, based on a report of a test after judgment.
rows.anchor: وتوقفت طائفة فيهم ومن هؤلاء أبو حنيفة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن شداد
rows.claim: A report from ʿAbd Allah b. Shaddad says polytheist children are tested after the final judgment: some obey the order to enter the fire and are assigned to the saved ranks, while those who refuse are cast into it.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن شداد أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أتاه رجل فسأله عن ذراري المشركين

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The verified scholars hold, and the author calls correct, that children of polytheists belong to Paradise; they cite this verse’s rule against punishment before moral obligation.
rows.anchor: وذهب المحققون إلى أنهم من أهل الجنة وهو الصحيح

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: They also cite the Prophet seeing Abraham in Paradise surrounded by human children; when asked whether they included polytheist children, the report is affirmative in the account cited from Bukhari.
rows.anchor: ومنها حديث إبراهيم الخليل عليه السلام حين رآه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في الجنة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report from Anas says that when asked about children of polytheists, the Prophet replied that they are servants of the people of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وابن عبد البر عن أنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse implies no punishment before obligation, and newborns cannot be obligated until maturity; scholars do not dispute that Muslim children are in Paradise.
rows.anchor: ومنها الآية الآتية حيث أفادت أن لا تعذيب قبل التكليف ولا يتوجه على المولود التكليف

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When Aisha called a deceased Ansari child a bird of Paradise, the Prophet cautioned against certainty and said God created people for Paradise or Hell while they were in their fathers’ loins.
rows.anchor: توفي صبي من الأنصار فقلت : طوبى له عصفور من عصافير الجنة

rows.speaker: العلماء
rows.claim: Scholars explain the rebuke either as warning against a definitive claim without proof, or as an earlier statement before the Prophet learned that Muslim children enter Paradise; other reports promise Paradise to Muslims whose three young children die.
rows.anchor: وأجاب العلماء عنه بأنه لعله عليه الصلاة والسلام نهاها عن المسارعة إلى القطع

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi argues that sin cannot be God’s act because then the servant would not be accountable; sin requires choice and ability to avoid it, which is why a child is not called a sinner.
rows.anchor: دلت الآية على أن الوزر ليس من فعله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qadi’s argument only answers determinists, not the mainstream position that denies both compulsion and total delegation.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن هذا إنما ينتهض على الجبرية لا على الجماعة القائلين لا جبر ولا تفويض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We would not punish” means divine wisdom and decree do not permit punishment, worldly or otherworldly, for any act or omission before a messenger guides, warns, establishes proofs, and lays down law.
rows.anchor: أي وما صح وما استقام منا بل استحال في سنتنا المبنية على الحكم البالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condition may require a messenger’s message to reach a person, even if the person was not individually addressed; the verse sets the endpoint of the period when punishment is not possible.
rows.anchor: حتى نبعث رسولا كذلك تبلغه دعوته سواء كان مبعوثا إليه أم لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse concerns the appointed time for punishment, not a ban on later punishment: afterlife punishment follows culpable deeds, as Noah’s people were punished only after a long delay.
rows.anchor: ألا يرى إلى قوم نوح عليه السلام كيف تأخر عنهم ما حل بهم زهاء ألف سنة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Muʿtazilites who affirm rational duties use the verse against themselves: if neglecting such duties necessarily warrants punishment, that would entail punishment before prophetic warning.
rows.anchor: وألزم المعتزلة القائلون بالوجوب بشرط ترك الواجب عندهم

rows.speaker: الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Al-Isfahani’s objections begin by reading “messenger” as reason, then argue the verse might exclude only direct punishment, not every form of punishment; the discussion continues in the next segment.
rows.anchor: وأورد الأصفهاني في شرح المحصول على من استدل بالآية

rows.speaker: الأصفهاني
rows.claim: Al-Isfahani’s objections include that the verse may not cover every sin, and that absent punishment does not disprove deserved punishment because forgiveness could remove it.
rows.anchor: على نفي التعذيب قبلها عن كل الذنوب الرابع أنا سلمنا الدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The replies take “messenger” literally as prophet, infer universal scope from “anyone,” and say absence of punishment before the message indicates no prior obligation; this fourth answer is especially effective against Muʿtazilites who reject pardon.
rows.anchor: ثم أجاب عن الأول بأن حقيقة الرسول هو النبي المرسل

rows.speaker: المراغي
rows.claim: Al-Maraghi offers a non-dialectical argument: even if obligation need not result in punishment, it must at least leave punishment possible, and the verse supposedly removes that insecurity.
rows.anchor: لا حاجة إلى جعل الدليل إلزاميا بل يجوز إتمامه على تقدير جواز العفو أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects this because insecurity is absent only when other evidence guarantees safety; before the verse, punishment could remain possible, so the inference does not establish that rational duty was absent.
rows.anchor: ورد ذلك أولا بمنع أن عدم الأمن من وقوع العذاب من لوازم ترك الواجب مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposal makes the consequent “punishment is permitted”; the author replies that the verse’s wording negates occurrence, not permission, so that inference fails.
rows.anchor: ورد بأن الملازمة القائلة لو كان الوجوب ثابتا قبل الشرع لعذب تارك الواجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads “We would not punish” as negating permissibility, a common force of “ما كنا”; if only nonoccurrence were meant, the wording would say “we do not punish.”
rows.anchor: وفيه معنى ما كنا معذبين ما سمعت وهو يدل على نفي الجواز

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues the verse cannot disprove rational duties: without an antecedent duty to hear a claimant and examine his miracle, prophethood cannot be established; making that duty scriptural creates circularity or regress.
rows.anchor: إذا جاء الشارع وادعى كونه نبيا من عند الله تعالى وأظهر المعجزة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s second argument is that a legal command or prohibition carries a threat of punishment for disobedience, and grounding this duty in scripture rather than reason again entails regress.
rows.anchor: فلا معنى للإيجاب والتحريم إلا أن يقول لو تركت كذا أو فعلت كذا لعاقبتك

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: His third argument says that because Sunnis permit pardon, obligation exists without actual punishment; it must therefore consist in fear of punishment or blame, which reason can produce.
rows.anchor: إن مذهب أهل السنة أنه يجوز من الله تعالى العفو عن العقاب على ترك الواجب

rows.speaker: العبادي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAbbadi answers that a miracle confirms the prophet’s truth, so accepting his report is obligatory without circularity; the established messenger can authoritatively convey revealed duties.
rows.anchor: إذا أظهر المعجزة على دعواه أنه رسول ثبت صدقه

rows.speaker: السيد السند
rows.claim: Al-Sayyid al-Sanad says scripture and the duty to follow are established by a messenger’s claim plus miracle when a rational addressee can examine it; customary knowledge after such examination means no delay is required.
rows.anchor: يثبت الشرع وتجب المتابعة بمجرد دعوى الرسالة مع اقتران المعجزة

rows.speaker: العبادي
rows.claim: For al-Razi’s second proof, avoiding punishment is not independent of duty; it is the duty itself or its consequence, so no regress follows.
rows.anchor: وجوب الاحتراز عن العقاب ليس أمرا أجنبيا عن وجوب كذا

rows.speaker: العبادي
rows.claim: For the third proof, fear may motivate performance but is not required for the act to occur; if the claim is about binding duty, its dependence on fear is simply denied.
rows.anchor: إنا لا نسلم أن الاتيان بالواجب متوقف على حصول الخوف
